source: de Groot (1946/1978) Thought and Choice in Chess, 2nd ed., Ch. 5-7 (Section 52, p. 266-274)
finding: De Groot defines progressive deepening. A move, plan or variant is investigated in successive phases. The same variant is taken up again and calculated further than before, either right away or after other moves. The investigation both broadens (new branches) and literally deepens (same line, more plies). He says it appears only in lengthy thought processes on hard choice problems.
numbers: Worked example, protocol (M2; Br): 78 protocol lines, five deepening phases (lines 1-19, 20-35, 36-48, 49-61, 62-78). The first move 1...R-N1 reappears in every phase, twice non-immediately in phase 2. Most long protocols divide into four phases.
quote: the same variant is taken up anew and is calculated further than before
limits: Based on protocols of 1938-1943 with a few dozen subjects; phase boundaries are partly subjective (his own statement). Only long processes show the structure clearly.
agent_relevance: Direct template for an S4/S5 loop that revisits the same candidate at greater depth, not only a new candidate. Our tree limit (3 children, depth 2) should allow re-entry into an already-visited node with a bigger depth budget.

source: de Groot (1978) Thought and Choice in Chess, Section 52 and Figure 7
finding: The four phases and what each does. 1 Orientation: look at the position, form a first judgement, note possibilities. 2 Exploration: try a few sample variations a few moves deep; if poor, put the move aside temporarily. 3 Investigation: deeper, more directed, more exhaustive search; more variants and more depth. 4 Proof: check and recapitulate, build a subjectively convincing argument, seek completeness.
numbers: In Figure 7 the same moves (for example 1...P-KR4 and 1...B-KN4) are cursory in phase 2 and several moves deep in phase 3.
quote: It is, in fact, the gradual increase in the subject's proving power requirements that brings about the phenomenon of progressive deepening.
limits: The four-phase scheme is a descriptive summary. De Groot says the real rules for move generation, stopping, evaluation and decision change subtly with the goal, more than four boxes suggest.
agent_relevance: Maps onto our states: orientation to S1-S2, exploration to S3-S4 with shallow budget, investigation to S4-S5 with larger budget on the leader, proof to S8 VERIFY. Proof is a separate check on the chosen line before output, which supports G3.

source: de Groot (1978) Section 52 points 1-3, the mechanism of scrapping a possibility
finding: Why a move is dropped, and why it comes back. A move is dropped when results fall below the maximal expectancy. Rejection is easier when the proving power of the bad result is high. Proving power depends on completeness of the analysis, size of the shortfall, uncertainty of end-position evaluation, and reliability of the expectation. The amount of proving power the player demands rises with the phase, and that rising demand is what drives deepening. Risky or calculation-heavy lines are deferred early, to avoid massive calculation.
numbers: No counts. Qualitative rules a to d under point 2 and a to d under point 3. Example: subject M1 sets aside 1.BxN/5 because 'I don't have to figure out all the variants' if another move proves stronger.
quote: The stage of progressive deepening determines, as it were, the approximate amount of energy to be spent on a particular investigation.
limits: Theory built from think-aloud reports. De Groot admits 'exhaustive' is relative and that even final arguments are usually incomplete and finished by an intuitive, emotional completion.
agent_relevance: A concrete stop and revisit rule for code: a candidate is dropped only with a stated shortfall against an expectation; the required proof strength grows by stage; end positions should be 'quiet' (no pending captures) before they are scored. This is a better-specified version of 'revise only on a signal' (G1, G2).

source: de Groot (1978) Section 36, Tables 2-6: protocol statistics
finding: Counting variables from the sequence of 'solving propositions' (which base move is under study). N = fresh starts, n = successive solving propositions, n0 = different moves considered. N-n = immediate re-investigations (c); n-n0 = non-immediate re-investigations (r). A thought process looks at few different moves but returns to them often.
numbers: 49 protocols, mean duration 14.6 min (range 0 to 35). Position A (19 protocols): N 8.4, n 6.2, n0 4.8, out of 56 legal moves. All main series: N 9.2, n 6.8, n0 4.5. So re-investigations (c+r) averaged almost 4, about equal to the number of different moves. The median of N-n0 is 3. Only two protocols had N-n0 = 0. First phase takes 23.5% of lines, about 3.2 min.
quote: the number of re-investigations in a protocol averaged over all protocols of the main series is almost four, the same as the average number of different moves considered
limits: Small sample, 1938-43 positions, thinking aloud for 10 to 30 minutes. De Groot warns the first-phase figures are partly an artefact of the setup.
agent_relevance: Gives a human benchmark: about 4-5 distinct candidates and about as many revisits per hard decision, a fresh start about every 1.5 minutes. A scaffold that revisits each of 3 candidates at most once or twice is in the human range. Revisits are normal, not a sign of failure.

source: de Groot (1978) Section 36, Position C and the weakest-subject protocols
finding: How often a player returns depends on the position type, and some weak players never return. Position C (not solvable by plan or by one line, only by comparing tried moves) produced the most revisiting. Weak subject W2 passed many moves in review but never returned to one: 'no progressive deepening', which de Groot calls a shortcoming of thought organisation.
numbers: Position C: c = 4.2 vs total mean 2.4; r = 3.8 vs 1.9; mr = 3.2 vs 2.1. Subject W2: A protocol T = 28 min, N = 10, n = 9, n0 = 9, so r = 0; C protocol T = 20 min, N = 11, n = 8, n0 = 8, r = 0. Extreme revisit protocols: (G5;B2) N 20, (M2;C) N 30, (M4;C) N 21.
quote: Many moves pass in review, but the subject never returns to a move previously considered. There is no progressive deepening
limits: Two weak players only; no statistic. Later replication (Gobet 1998) found maximal non-immediate revisits fall with skill, so weak players there did return more (see a12).
agent_relevance: Revisiting a candidate with new depth is a mark of good organisation in de Groot's reading; pure breadth (list many, never return) is the weak pattern. Supports an operator for 'return to leader with larger budget'.

source: de Groot (1978) Ch. 9, Tables 11-12: five grandmasters vs five experts on position A
finding: The central result. Grandmasters and experts do not differ much in the macro-structure of search. Depth of calculation cannot be the main difference. Grandmasters picked far better moves, and were somewhat faster and mentioned more moves per minute. De Groot infers the difference is qualitative (what is selected), found in the first seconds.
numbers: Position A, 5 G vs 5 E. Mean time 9.6 vs 12.8 min. Fresh starts N 6.6 vs 6.4. Different first moves n0 4.2 vs 3.4. Max depth Dmax 6.8 vs 6.6 plies. Moves mentioned M 35.0 vs 30.8. Moves per minute 3.5 vs 2.5. Different first moves per minute 0.49 vs 0.29. Move quality R 8.2 vs 5.2 (scale to 9). Table 11: c 1.8 vs 2.0, r 0.6 vs 1.0.
quote: It is thus beyond doubt that the depth of calculation cannot be the prime distinguishing characteristic between the grandmaster and the expert player.
limits: Five per group, large overlap, one position that is solvable to 9 plies (Campitelli and Gobet 2004 show an easy position hides search differences). De Groot himself says differences exist but are not in these statistics.
agent_relevance: For a scaffold: quality comes from choosing what to look at, not from raw depth. Spend effort on candidate selection and evaluation of end positions before adding depth. Matches G11/G12 (do not add thinking blindly).

source: de Groot (1978) Ch. 8-9: perception experiments and Section 36 on subject M2
finding: Where the skill difference does show up: reproduction of a position after a few seconds. Grandmasters and masters reproduce about 93%, experts 68%, class players 51%. De Groot also notes individual style: master M2 'tries out' many more variations than other masters (N 21, n0 11, with the next highest n0 being 9).
numbers: 14 positions, 2 to 15 s exposure. Total correct: G 93%, M 93%, E 68%, C 51% (defect 6.6%, 8.6%, 30.4%, 47.5%). Homogeneous 10 positions, mean 3.2-3.85 s: G 92%, M 92%, E 71%, C 47%. One subject per class (Euwe as G).
limits: One subject per skill class in the perception test. This is the chunking subfield; only cited here for contrast with flat search statistics.
agent_relevance: Skill sits in fast recognition of the position, not in search volume. Argues for giving the agent a strong cheap first pass (S1-S2 representation, recall of known templates) before search.

source: de Groot (1978) Ch. 11 Epilogue, programming implications
finding: De Groot argues chess programs need cyclic progressive deepening with goal feedback, not one fixed generator, stop rule and evaluation. He says the crucial improvement is to simulate the development of the total goal conception by repeated cycles, and notes this means waiving the old restraint that a move is investigated only once. He compares it with empirical science: try the favourite small-scale, try a second method, return to the first more thoroughly, then try to prove it.
numbers: No counts. He estimates the main gain from better goal-setting, with diminishing payoff from refining the evaluation function.
quote: the crucial principle for the improvement of chess playing programs is to simulate the development of the human subject's total goal (problem) conception by employing the strategy of cyclic, progressive deepening.
limits: A 1965/1978 programming opinion. Computer chess later succeeded mainly by brute-force alpha-beta plus iterative deepening, a different thing (see a24).
agent_relevance: Historic root of the iterative-deepening idea in AI. For our agent the useful point is the loop: each cycle changes the goal and criteria (what counts as enough proof), not just the depth number.

source: de Groot (1978) Section 32/Section 52 on immediate vs non-immediate re-investigation (p. 171-173)
finding: Two kinds of return. Immediate re-investigation (same move in the next episode) mostly clarifies a result just obtained. Non-immediate re-investigation, after other moves, mostly serves overall deepening. Reasons for a return include a detected error, lowered expectations, or a new idea to strengthen the old plan. The pattern of letters for moves reveals phases, for example (g-a-e)-(a-a-k)-(a-i)-a-a.
numbers: Example formula (M1;A): g-a-e-a-a-k-a-i-a-a, with a = 1.BxN/5. In 15% of all protocols the final move played was not the last one investigated; in position A only 1 of 19 (5%).
limits: Interpretation by the author from protocol text; he marks borderline cases where the return adds nothing new, for example from despair or fatigue.
agent_relevance: Distinguish two operators in code: 'extend this branch' (immediate) and 'return to the old leader with new information' (non-immediate). Log the move-letter sequence per run; it is a cheap trace of whether the agent really deepens or only loops.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited, Swiss Journal of Psychology 57, 18-32
finding: Direct replication of de Groot's position A with 48 Swiss players (12 each at Master 2317, Expert 2101, class A 1903, class B 1699 Elo). Skill differences were larger than de Groot found, but still small: Masters choose better moves, take a shorter first phase, look at fewer base moves and search slightly deeper on average. No difference in nodes, maximal depth, time, or rate of nodes.
numbers: Mean depth (plies) 5.0, 4.6, 3.7, 2.9 (F(3,44)=2.9, p<.05, only Master vs class B). Regression mean depth = -2.638 + 0.003 x Elo, about 0.6 ply per 200 Elo. Nodes 58.0, 58.3, 56.8, 33.9 (ns). Max depth 9.1 plies for masters vs 8 pooled (ns). Base moves 3.2 (Masters) vs 6.5 (class A), p<.05. First phase 1.1, 2.3, 1.6, 4.2 min (p=.01). Time 11.3 min Masters vs 16.7 others (ns).
limits: Position A is easy (decisive advantage visible within 9 plies). Study run in 1986 as a post-test of a controllability experiment; audio taping vs de Groot's note taking. Single position, men only, no world-class group.
agent_relevance: Weak players spread across many first moves (up to 9-11) while masters look at 1-3. Scaffold analogue: cap the number of base candidates and force depth on few, rather than many shallow tries.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited, regression and partialling analyses
finding: Search variables explain only part of move quality, and skill still predicts quality after search is removed, which points to knowledge or pattern recognition. Total time was a (tiny) negative predictor, mean depth a positive one.
numbers: Stepwise regression: Move quality = 2.429 - 0.001 x TotalTime + 0.304 x MeanDepth + 0.188 x MaxNumberRI; R2 = 35.1%. Elo alone R2 = 29.2%. After partialling out mean depth, max depth and nodes, Elo still explained 17.6% (p<.005). For recall, Elo explained 72.3% of variance (Gobet & Simon 1996, n=25).
limits: Move quality is a 5-point rating by the author and de Groot. Elo explains little because variability is high. Not a causal test.
agent_relevance: More thinking time did not buy quality in this task (coefficient about zero): consistent with G11. Depth helps a little; knowledge helps more.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited, re-investigation results and comparison with de Groot
finding: Progressive deepening replicated in 48 players, with a skill twist. Masters do more immediate returns and almost no non-immediate returns; weaker players jump around more. Swiss sample overall did not differ from de Groot's sample on any variable tested.
numbers: Max number of immediate re-investigations rises with skill, F(3,44)=5.91, p<.005. Max number of non-immediate re-investigations falls with skill, F(3,44)=3.71, p<.02 (Masters differ only from class A). Overall re-investigations: Masters and others not significant, F=0.67. Pooled immediate re-investigations 3.2 (Swiss) vs 2.4 (de Groot); non-immediate 1.6 vs 1.2; first phase 2.3 vs 3.1 min. Best move chosen in about one third of protocols in both samples.
limits: Contradicts the simple de Groot reading in a5 that weak players do not return. Authors flag the audio vs note taking artefact. No meta-analysis possible because de Groot gives few usable protocols per level (three Master, two class).
agent_relevance: Strong play looks like: finish one line properly (immediate), then pick the next; weaker play looks like hopping back and forth. So deepening should be disciplined: return only on a stated reason (G1), not by drift.

source: Gobet (1998) Chess players' thinking revisited, introduction and discussion
finding: Collects the earlier evidence on depth vs skill and names the competing explanations. Pattern-recognition models (Chase and Simon, Gobet and Simon) predict small search differences; search models (Holding's SEEK) predict large ones. Gobet argues the contrast is false, and that for experts the key question is when to stop searching, which pattern recognition answers by evaluating positions.
numbers: Charness (1981): about 0.5 ply of mean depth per 200 Elo (sample 1284-2004 Elo). Saariluoma (1990, 10-min limit): inverted U, Masters (about 2200) 52 nodes at 5.1 plies vs IM and GM 23 nodes at 3.6 plies. De Groot: grandmasters seldom look at more than 100 continuations. Class A outlier searched 23 plies and 'did not know when to stop'.
quote: the critical question is not: 'How to search as deep as possible?' but: 'When to stop searching?'
limits: Secondary account of Charness 1981 and Saariluoma 1990 (those papers not opened by us). Gobet's own interpretive position.
agent_relevance: Stopping is the hard design problem. A stop rule that depends on a reliable evaluation of a quiet end position (code-checkable test results in our case) matches the human solution.

source: Campitelli & Gobet (2004) Adaptive expert decision making: skilled chess players search more and deeper, ICGA Journal 27(4), 209-216
finding: With hard positions that need deep search, there is a large and linear skill effect in search, and absolute depths and node counts are 2 to 10 times higher than in de Groot-style studies. Authors conclude earlier work vastly underestimated expert search potential, and that players adapt method to task demands.
numbers: N=4 (GM 2550, IM 2500, CM 2100, class B 1750), 3 positions, 30 min limit. Mean depth (plies): 13.8, 10.5, 7.4, 2.8. Max depth: 25, 23.7, 17.7, 10.5. Nodes: 370, 405, 152.7, 88. Nodes per min: 12.3, 13.5, 6.8, 3.2. Regressions: mean depth = -18.3 + 0.012 Elo (2.4 plies per 200 Elo, vs 0.5 Charness, 0.6 Gobet 1998); max depth = -19.9 + 0.018 Elo. Positions needed at least 52, 60, 70 nodes and 23, 25, 35 plies. De Groot position A needs only 17 nodes and 9 plies.
limits: Only four participants, one per level, so regression is from 4 points. Positions B and C had unique wins and players were told to find them (instruction differs from de Groot). Position C data of class B lost.
agent_relevance: Task difficulty decides whether depth matters. Easy item: pattern recognition, little search. Hard item that truly needs a long forced line: strong players search 10+ plies. Our budget-by-difficulty rule (G12) fits; depth limits must rise on tasks that need it.

source: Campitelli & Gobet (2004), supplementary tasks: fast decisions, recall, practice
finding: The same four players behaved like pattern-recognition theory predicts on fast, memory and practice tasks, so the deep search is not a different kind of expert. Skill effect remained when search time was almost removed.
numbers: 49 positions (mean 10.4 nodes, 6.4 plies), 5 s view then 10 s to answer: GM 23 correct (46.9%), IM 18 (36.9%), CM 4 (8.2%), CB 2 (4.1%), r(4)=.94. Recall of game positions 5 s: 83.2%, 85%, 54%, 47%; random 21.7, 19, 17.7, 15.5; shapes about 15 each. Study hours: 6890, 7904, 1872, 416; play hours 7722, 7072, 2704, 1326. No skill effect in a reaction-time task.
limits: N=4. Fast-decision positions chosen by authors from Livshitz.
agent_relevance: One mechanism, two modes: a fast recognition answer when the item is familiar, and extended search when it is not. Suggests S0 GATE should route familiar items to a quick answer.

source: Campitelli & Gobet (2004), section 4: qualitative features and Kotov's method
finding: Kotov's trainer advice (list candidates, analyse each to an evaluation once, never jump between branches) differs from what de Groot saw (everyone, even grandmasters, reinvestigates). In 2004 protocols, class B and candidate master jumped with no candidate list; GM also jumped but kept an expandable candidate list and tried to stay disciplined; the IM followed Kotov's textbook method. Conclusion: search is not restricted to progressive deepening but can be under strategic control.
numbers: One player per level (N=4). Both GM and IM had read Kotov.
quote: search behaviour is not restricted to progressive deepening but can be under strategic control
limits: Qualitative, n=1 per level; GM called his own jumping undisciplined.
agent_relevance: Two search disciplines exist and a program can pick: Kotov (one candidate list, finish each branch) vs progressive deepening (shallow pass over all, return deeper). Testable as two operator policies at equal tokens (G7).

source: Connors, Burns & Campitelli (2011) Expertise in complex decision making: the role of search in chess 70 years after de Groot, Cognitive Science 35(8), 1567-1579
finding: Abstract only (full text paywalled; fetch blocked). Think-aloud replication with 22 players on two positions. Stronger players searched faster; both top groups searched far faster than in earlier studies. Authors say results still support de Groot and pattern-recognition models.
numbers: 6 grandmasters, 5 international masters, 6 experts, 5 class A. Two positions. Detailed means not seen.
limits: Abstract level only; do not quote numbers from it. Needs full-text check in a later pass.
agent_relevance: Third replication direction: speed of search rises with skill, depth claims uncertain. Keep as a lead for Angle B/C agents.

source: Gobet (1997) A pattern-recognition theory of search in expert problem solving, Thinking & Reasoning 3, 291-313 (SEARCH model)
finding: SEARCH is a probabilistic computer model of search built on chunks and templates. Moves come from recognition (fast) or weak heuristics (slow). A move is made in the mind's eye, then recognition runs on the new image. Evaluation is done at terminal positions only. An episode stops when error risk (forgetting, interference) is too high, when expectation is met, or on a decisive event.
numbers: Time costs: 2 s to make a move in the mind's eye, 10 s to evaluate by heuristics. Rules for choosing the next base move include: re-search a line if its evaluation was unreliable; re-search it to store it in long-term memory; prefer normal base moves early and unusual ones late (after Newell & Simon 1972); continue if favourable, switch if unfavourable.
limits: The model computes depth, rate and fuzziness, but does not play chess. Parameters are set by the author and simulated, not fitted line by line.
agent_relevance: A formal reason for progressive deepening: a line is revisited because the first evaluation was unreliable or to consolidate memory. For an LLM the equivalent of mind's eye decay is context drift; re-searching a line from a clean restatement is the analogue.

source: Gobet (1997) SEARCH model simulations of depth and rate vs skill
finding: SEARCH predicts that mean depth and rate of search follow a power function of the number of chunks, so depth grows slowly with skill. That explains the small depth differences in de Groot, Charness and Gobet 1998, and the inverted-U in Saariluoma as sampling variability.
numbers: Mean depth about under 1 ply with no chunks, 2.5 plies at 1,000 chunks, 4 plies at about 30,000 chunks (expert), above 5 plies beyond 100,000 chunks (grandmaster). Holding's analysis of de Groot: experts 4.8, grandmasters 5.3 plies. Charness regression gives 2.3 plies (1300 Elo), 4.1 (2000), 5.7 (GM). Fitted curve in figure: y = 1.073 x^0.133, r2 = 0.945.
limits: Predicts a ceiling-like slow growth; Campitelli and Gobet 2004 found a far steeper rise on hard positions, which the authors say SEARCH underestimates. Power-law shape rests on an assumed constant learning rate.
agent_relevance: Prior for depth schedules: returns diminish with knowledge; most gain is from selectivity. Do not set very deep default budgets for an agent with strong priors.

source: Gobet & Charness (2006) Expertise in chess, in Cambridge Handbook of Expertise and Expert Performance
finding: Review of search and progressive deepening. Progressive deepening happens both to compensate for memory limits and to pass information from one branch to another. Depth rises with skill up to expert (Charness 1981), but a nine-year study of one player found no depth gain from 1600 to 2300 Elo.
numbers: Charness (1989) longitudinal case: 1600 to 2300 rating in nine years, no significant depth increase. Null moves (missing moves for one side) about 12% of moves (Saariluoma and Hohlfeld 1994) and 10% (Charness 1981). Kasparov simultaneous play ranked him among the six best in the world. Blunders per 1,000 moves: 5.02 classical vs 6.85 rapid (Chabris and Hearst 2003).
limits: Narrative review, no fresh data. Opinionated toward pattern recognition.
agent_relevance: Two named reasons for revisiting (memory support and information propagation) correspond to two LLM motives: context loss and passing a learned fact between branches. Null-move thinking (plan for one side only) is a cheap abstraction an agent could use.

source: Gobet & Charness (2006) Expertise in chess, on stereotyped solutions and Holding-Reynolds task
finding: Strong players lean on stereotyped solutions: in tactical positions they chose familiar longer mates and missed shorter odd ones (Saariluoma 1990, 1992). Skill gave better moves after minutes of thought but not better recall after a short view (Holding and Reynolds 1982); when recall was asked after solving, stronger players recalled better (Schultetus and Charness 1999), read as new chunks formed during search.
numbers: No new numbers; see sources.
limits: Secondary source for the original experiments (not opened).
agent_relevance: Search itself creates new patterns that help later steps; revisiting a line after solving a sub-part benefits from the learned pattern. Also a warning: familiar solutions crowd out better ones (see a25).

source: Gobet & Simon (1998) Pattern recognition makes search possible: comments on Holding (1992), Psychological Research 61, 204-208
finding: Rebuttal of Holding's SEEK (Search, Evaluation, Knowledge) theory. Chase and Simon never said forward search can be ignored: perceptual chunks guide the search and hold its results. Valid criticisms (chunk size, speed of long-term storage) were fixed by template theory. The mind's eye loop is: make the move internally, re-perceive, new patterns suggest new moves.
numbers: Chunk learning about 8 s per chunk, short-term memory about seven chunks; Simon and Gilmartin estimate 10,000 to 100,000 chunks for expertise; chunks of up to 17 pieces for masters (Gobet and Simon, in press).
quote: When the move is made in the mind's eye ... the result is then passed back through the pattern perception system and new patterns are perceived.
limits: A rebuttal by the theory's authors; SEEK was never formalised, which weakens the comparison.
agent_relevance: Model of search as a recognise-act loop. For an LLM: each step re-reads the updated state rather than relying on an earlier summary.

source: Gobet & Simon (1996) The roles of recognition processes and look-ahead search in time-constrained expert problem solving, Psychological Science 7, 52-55
finding: Natural experiment on time pressure. Kasparov played simultaneous matches with 4 to 8 team opponents, roughly one quarter to one eighth of normal move time. His performance rating dropped by only about 100 Elo points. Authors read this as recognition doing most of the work. The paper cites de Groot's finding that stronger and weaker players examine about the same number of branches (about 100 branches in 15 min, about 9 s per branch).
numbers: Ten matches 1985-1992. Performances from 2310 to 2786, opponents' mean Elo 2320 to 2550; example of formula 2450 + 400(4.5 - 1.5)/6 = 2650 vs his usual level about 2750. No correlation between number of opponents and performance.
limits: Later criticised: no information on variability; Chabris and Hearst found rapid and blindfold games had more blunders than classical (6.85 and 7.63 vs 5.02 per 1,000 moves, a reliable difference). Opponents were national teams, not a controlled design.
agent_relevance: Shrinking the thinking budget by a large factor costs little for an expert on familiar material. Supports short default thinking (G11), but also shows a measurable cost, so the budget should go up when the item is hard.

source: Gobet (2003) Forward search, pattern recognition and visualization in expert chess: a reply to Chabris and Hearst (2003)
finding: Disagreement on how to read time-pressure data. Chabris and Hearst: grandmasters make more blunders when time is cut (blunder = move 1.5 pawns below an engine's best), so search matters. Gobet: a six-fold cut in time raising blunders only from 5.02 to 6.85 per 1,000 supports pattern recognition. Both sides agree the two must be combined.
numbers: Chabris and Hearst data (Monaco tournaments, six editions): 5.02 blunders per 1,000 moves classical (about 3 min per move), 6.85 rapid (under 30 s), 7.63 blindfold. Significant: classical vs rapid and vs blindfold; rapid vs blindfold not. Kasparov simultaneous median performance 2682 Elo, interquartile range 203.5 (four extra matches). De Groot quoted: after five seconds Euwe was further in understanding than a strong amateur after fifteen minutes.
limits: Commentary, not a new experiment. 'Same data, opposite reading' shows effect-size interpretation, not data, is contested.
agent_relevance: Shows the right design: compare quality at several time budgets with an engine-like ground truth. We can do this exactly with benchmark items and token budgets.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Inflexibility of experts: quantifying the Einstellung effect in chess masters, Cognitive Psychology
finding: Boundary condition for deepening. When a familiar good solution exists, experts stop at it and fail to find a shorter one, even though all of them said they were looking for better. The more expert, the less the effect. The effect cut ordinary experts to the level of players three standard deviations lower.
numbers: Group 1, 2-solution problem: all grandmasters found the shorter solution; 50% of IMs, 18% of Masters (two Masters), 0% of candidate masters did (all of them found it in the 1-solution version). Experts guessed 86%, 74%, 59% for IM, Master, CM. Logistic regression on Elo: B=.013, p=.004; 100 fewer Elo points cut the odds of finding it by a factor of 3.67; model probabilities .64 (Elo 2550), .32 (2450), .12 (2350), .01 (2150). Non-finders spent about 8-9 s looking.
limits: Small groups; one experiment type (smothered mate vs shorter line). Instruction asked for the shortest solution. Only the first few seconds of extra search were tested.
agent_relevance: Returning to a candidate does not guarantee a better idea: a revisit can just confirm the first idea. G8 and G3 fit: a revisit must use a new test or new framing, not the same line again.

source: Bilalic, McLeod & Gobet (2008) Why good thoughts block better ones: the mechanism of the pernicious Einstellung effect, Cognition
finding: Eye tracking shows what looks like extra search is not. After finding the familiar mate, candidate masters said they were hunting for a shorter solution, but kept looking at the squares tied to the familiar line the whole time; players without the familiar option looked more and more at the squares of the optimal line.
numbers: Candidate masters, eye-tracked, two groups. Group on the 2-solution problem: share of time on familiar-line squares did not change over six time periods (F(5,20)=0.6, ns). Group on the 1-solution problem: shift toward optimal-line squares, F(5,20)=11.9, p<.001, partial eta2 = .75. Smothered mate took about 37 s (SD 20) to find.
limits: Small groups (interaction tests on 5 and 20 df), one problem family. Candidate masters only.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G10: what the agent says it is doing in a retry (look for an alternative) is not what its attention does. A revisit should be forced to cover different material, for example by masking the first solution or requiring a different mechanism.

source: Kotov (1971) Think Like a Grandmaster, as reported in Campitelli & Gobet (2004)
finding: Kotov's training method: choose the candidate moves first, analyse each until an evaluation is reached, do not repeat a variation or jump between branches; a new candidate only after the previous one is finished. Cited as a contrast to de Groot's finding that everyone revisits.
numbers: No numbers reported.
limits: Second-hand through Campitelli and Gobet 2004. The book was not opened.
agent_relevance: The 'depth-first, finish one candidate' policy. A candidate for a competing operator policy to test against progressive deepening.

source: Charness (1981) Search in chess: age and skill differences, as reported in Gobet (1998) and Campitelli & Gobet (2004)
finding: Reported by later papers: players from 1284 to 2004 Elo on four positions, 10-minute limit. Skill effects on move quality, mean depth, total moves, episodes and branches; none on rate of search. Re-analysis of de Groot found grandmasters generate more base moves per minute than experts. Charness suggested depth plateaus above expert level.
numbers: About 0.5 ply of mean depth per 200 Elo. Max depth about 1.5 plies per 200 Elo (as quoted by Campitelli and Gobet). Plateau claim not supported by 2004 data.
limits: Second-hand. Time cap of 10 min may have limited depth; positions differ from de Groot's.
agent_relevance: Gives the first quantified slope for the 'how much deeper do stronger solvers go' question.

source: Holding (1985) The psychology of chess skill; Holding (1992) Theories of chess skill, SEEK theory, as reported in Gobet (1998) and Gobet & Simon (1998)
finding: Competing account: chess skill is Search, Evaluation and Knowledge. Stronger players search deeper; de Groot's null result may have had too little statistical power. Holding computed average depth from de Groot's data: experts 4.8, grandmasters 5.3 plies. Holding predicted a roughly linear rise of search with skill.
numbers: Holding on de Groot: 4.8 vs 5.3 plies (via Gobet 1997). Holding and Reynolds (1982) found skill predicted move choice after minutes but not recall after 8 s.
limits: Second-hand. SEEK was never made precise enough for quantitative prediction (Gobet and Simon 1998).
agent_relevance: The 'depth really matters' position, whose slope claim (linear) is closer to the 2004 data than the plateau claim.

source: Newell & Simon (1972) Human Problem Solving, chess episodes and problem behavior graphs, as used in Gobet (1998) and Gobet (1997)
finding: Source of the problem behavior graph used to code chess protocols into episodes and nodes, and of the rules in SEARCH: favour normal moves early and unusual moves later, continue an episode if the result is favourable and switch if not, stop when an expectation is met. Chase & Simon (1973) put perception chunks into this search frame.
numbers: Wagner and Scurrah (1971) candidate master: about 10 nodes per minute and 172 nodes on average (per Campitelli and Gobet). Newell & Simon used only a handful of subjects (per Gobet 1998).
limits: Book not opened; only second-hand statements. Not checked directly.
agent_relevance: Formal vocabulary (episode, base move, node, problem behavior graph) we can reuse to log and compare agent search traces with human protocols.
